title: Naaman (2 Kings 5)
hook: a proud general is told to wash seven times in a muddy river

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chariot of fire, and Elisha picking up Elijah's fallen mantle. Your line was pick up the mantle.

The person who sets this story moving doesn't even get a name. She's a little girl from Israel, carried off by raiders from Syria, now a servant to the wife of the Syrian army's commander. That commander is Naaman: a great man, honored, brave, rich, and a leper. And one day this captive girl says to her mistress: I wish my master were with the prophet in Samaria. He would heal him. One sentence of kindness from a kidnapped child, and a general packs up silver, gold, ten changes of clothes, and a letter from his king.
screen: `A CAPTIVE GIRL FROM ISRAEL.` → `A GREAT GENERAL, AND A LEPER.` → `ONE SENTENCE OF KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Naaman arrives at Elisha's door with his horses and chariots, the full parade. And Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger with a short instruction, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go, and wash seven times in the Jordan." Naaman is furious. He'd pictured the prophet coming out, calling on his God, waving a hand over the spot, something worthy of a general. And the Jordan? Aren't the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel? He turns to leave in a rage. Then his servants gently say: "if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, surely thou shouldst have done it: how much rather what he now hath said to thee: Wash, and thou shalt be clean?" He asked for something simple. So Naaman goes down to the river and dips himself seven times. And his flesh, the Douay says, became "like the flesh of a little child." Like the girl who started all this. He goes back and says: now I know there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Elisha refuses any payment at all. Notice who carried the healing to Naaman: a captive girl, a messenger, his own servants. Jesus remembers him in the synagogue at Nazareth: many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time, and none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian. Catholic tradition sees baptism here: going down into the water, coming up like a newborn. The Church reads this story in Lent, as people prepare for baptism at Easter.
screen: `THE PROPHET DOESN'T COME OUT.` · `GO, AND WASH SEVEN TIMES.` · `IF HE'D ASKED A GREAT THING.` · `FLESH LIKE A LITTLE CHILD'S.` · then, large: `WASH, AND THOU SHALT BE CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Think of a problem where the answer is probably small, the apology you could just say, the doctor you could just call, the early night, and you've been waiting for something bigger. If a voice says that's too simple to matter, that's Naaman at the riverbank; if you pray, ask for the humility to go down to the water.
Naaman. The proud Syrian general healed of leprosy when he finally did the simple thing and washed seven times in the Jordan. Today's word.
Your line: go and wash. And that's week fifty-nine: wisdom, the Temple, the widow's jar, Carmel, the whisper, the mantle, and Naaman. Day four hundred thirteen, in the books.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-NINE: WISDOM · TEMPLE · THE JAR · CARMEL · WHISPER · MANTLE · NAAMAN`

howItsDone: Catholics hear Naaman's healing at Mass in Lent, alongside Jesus recalling him at Nazareth, and the Church has long read his washing in the Jordan as a figure of baptism.

original.note: Hebrew: the skin disease translated leprosy, a broader term than the disease called leprosy today.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle cure in a river.
what it means: a proud man is healed only when he accepts something simple, and the people who lead him there are a captive girl and his own servants.
what a scholar hears: tsara'at covers many skin conditions, not only modern leprosy; and Luke 4:27 has Jesus cite Naaman, a foreigner, at Nazareth.

chat.meaning: Naaman pictured something worthy of a general. His servants said: if he'd asked a great thing, you'd have done it. Wash, and be clean.

Week fifty-nine counted as days 407–413; confirm the look-back list.
Naaman's request to bow in the temple of Rimmon (5:18) and Gehazi's greed (5:20–27) are omitted.
Tsara'at as a broader term than Hansen's disease: standard; confirm.
'A small, muddy river' is interpretive; the text has Naaman compare the Jordan unfavorably with the Abana and Pharpar.
